corrected_value.title_o: Improving problem solving with subgoal labels in expository text and worked examples

decisions.quote:
Prior study to be replicated

In line with these predictions, Margulieux and Catrambone (2016) found that subgoal
labels improved learning for a programming task most if they were placed in the exposi-
tory text and worked examples.
decisions.location: Prior study to be replicated, p. 710, lines 182-186 (Reference list, p. 721, lines 789-791)
decisions.reason: The section explicitly titled 'Prior study to be replicated' identifies Margulieux and Catrambone (2016) (DOI: 10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.12.002) as the sole target study re-tested by Experiments 1 and 2. Both the shipped record and blind coding (target_index 0) identify this same original paper.

decisions.quote:
For both procedures that were studied, subgoal labeled worked examples had a consistent
effect: improved problem solving performance. These results align with the original Mar-
gulieux and Catrambone (2016) study and other previous research (e.g., Catrambone 1998;
Margulieux et al. 2016), suggesting that subgoal labels reliably help students learn from
worked examples more effectively. For subgoal labeled expository text, however, the effect
differed in both domains, and neither matched the pattern of results found in programming.
decisions.reason: Across both new experiments (statistics in Experiment 1 and chemistry in Experiment 2) re-testing Margulieux and Catrambone (2016), the authors explicitly report that the positive main effect of subgoal labeled worked examples aligned with the original study, whereas the interaction with subgoal labeled expository text did not replicate in either domain (showing no effect in statistics and an additive main effect without interaction in chemistry). Under the codebook, explicit agreement on one tested component alongside explicit contrast on another yields 'mixed', matching both the shipped and blind codings.

decisions.quote:
The present study used methods similar to those described in Margulieux and Catram-
bone (2016). In a laboratory experiment, participants were given abstract expository text
that explained how to solve problems and concrete worked examples that demonstrated
a problem being solved. Depending on their randomly assigned condition, participants
received subgoal labels in both, one or the other, or none of these instructional materi-
als. Subgoals of the procedure were determined using the task analysis by problem solving
(TAPS) procedure and consultation with subject-matter experts (Catrambone 2011) as is
typical in recent subgoal learning research (e.g., Margulieux and Catrambone 2016).
   It was hypothesized that the pattern of results in the new domains would replicate those
found in the programming domain. That is, subgoal labeled expository texts would interact
with subgoal labeled worked examples to produce the best problem solving performance.
decisions.reason: The paper collects new experimental data in two independent student samples (Experiment 1 in statistics, N=120; Experiment 2 in chemistry, N=120) to re-test the published findings of Margulieux and Catrambone (2016). Both shipped and blind codings accurately classify the record type as 'replication'.
